steps.text: A lizard is a living thing, and its sculpted, curving body is more than the tools can build. The closest version they can make is a flat articulated lizard: a side-view silhouette of segments, each one extruded flat on the bed, joined by pin hinges. The segments swing side to side in the plane, and the whole chain prints flat with no supports. I'll build it only after you pick a version.

steps.text: Your reply asked for common sizes and sensible defaults, so I'll take the flat articulated chain, the version that swings side to side, and set the sizes myself. I'll show them on a sheet for you to confirm before building.
The sizes are confirmed. Next I'll set out the build plan for the segment and its hinge.

assumptions: Segments are flat plates in the XY plane, printed flat, so no supports are needed
Each joint is a vertical pin (Z axis), so segments swing side to side in the plane
Joint clearance 0.4 mm so the hinge moves freely after printing
Seven segments, 20 mm long each, with a head and tail to reach about 150 mm total
A loose 2.5 mm pin is printed or inserted as a separate piece
questions: Should the pins be separate printed pieces or inserted by hand?

steps.text:
I built a first draft of the flat articulated lizard, and it needs work before it's a working hinge.

What's in the project: one segment (20 x 14 x 4 mm, with a 6 mm knuckle, a 2.5 mm pin bore and a 6.4 mm socket at the back), copied eight times at 20.4 mm pitch. The eight segments span about 153 mm, close to your 150 mm, so I used eight instead of the seven in the plan. The sizes you didn't set are my guesses: 20 mm segments, 14 mm width, 4 mm thickness, 2.5 mm pin, 0.4 mm clearance.

Two things are off:
- **The joints don't line up yet.** The socket center sits 0.4 mm away from the knuckle center on the neighbor, so the pin wouldn't pass straight through. The design check also failed on size and feature count, because it compared against the single-segment plan. Those failures reflect the eight-copy layout and the extra socket step, not a broken part.
- **It's not a printed-in-one-go chain.** The segments are separate pieces that would need a loose pin each, so the "print in one go" part of your request isn't met yet.

Nothing has been sliced or sent to a printer. Should I rework the joints so each pin runs through a concentric socket with a real clearance gap, then slice the plate for your P1S?
